subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: Each copy keeps one old strand; base pairing keeps the copy accurate
Helicase opens the helix; DNA polymerase builds the new strands
Using PCR and electrophoresis: DNA profiling in forensics and paternity
Four prokaryotic enzymes: primase, polymerase III, polymerase I, ligase
Transcription: RNA polymerase makes an RNA copy of one gene
Base pairing sets the RNA sequence; hydrogen bonds let it go
Transcription is where gene expression is switched on or off
What mRNA, the ribosome and tRNA each do
Reading an mRNA sequence with the codon table
Elongation: one codon, one peptide bond, one step along
Both transcription and translation run 5' to 3'
Most eukaryotic DNA does not code for polypeptides, but has functions
Pre-mRNA is spliced and capped before it leaves the nucleus
How translation starts, and the A, P and E sites
Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation

questions.q: Bacteria were grown for many generations with only heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N), so all their DNA was heavy. They were then moved to a medium with only light nitrogen (¹⁴N). After one round of replication, all the DNA had a density midway between heavy and light. After a second round, half the DNA was of this intermediate density and half was light. What do these results show about replication?
options: The original double-stranded molecule stays intact and a completely new molecule is made beside it.
Old and new nucleotides become mixed along both strands of every daughter molecule.
Each daughter molecule keeps one original strand and gains one strand that is newly made.
The DNA is not copied but is shared out equally between the daughter cells at each division.
optionWhy: A student who pictures conservative replication picks this. Conservative replication would give heavy and light DNA, never intermediate, after the first round; the observed intermediate density rules it out.

A student who pictures dispersive replication picks this. Mixing would fit the first round, but after the second round all molecules would be of a single, lighter intermediate density; no wholly light DNA would appear.

After one round every molecule is one heavy strand plus one light strand, giving intermediate density. After a second round, the two strands of each intermediate molecule separate again, giving half intermediate and half wholly light molecules. Only semi-conservative replication predicts both results.

A student who thinks DNA is halved at division picks this. If no new DNA were made, no light nitrogen could be incorporated and all the DNA would have stayed heavy; the shift to intermediate and then to light density shows that new strands were synthesized.
questions.explain: After one round every molecule is one heavy strand plus one light strand, giving intermediate density. After a second round, the two strands of each intermediate molecule separate again, giving half intermediate and half wholly light molecules. Only semi-conservative replication predicts both results.

questions.q: A drug inhibits helicase but has no effect on DNA polymerase. What will happen to DNA replication in a cell treated with the drug?
options: Replication cannot begin, because the hydrogen bonds between the strands are not broken, so no template strand is exposed.
Replication continues normally, because DNA polymerase unwinds the double helix itself as it copies each strand.
New strands are made but fall off the template, because helicase forms the hydrogen bonds that hold new bases in place.
Cell division continues without replication, because the existing DNA is simply shared between the two daughter cells.
optionWhy: Helicase is needed to unwind the helix and break the hydrogen bonds between the strands. Without it the strands stay paired, no template is exposed and DNA polymerase has nothing to copy.
A student who gives the unwinding job to DNA polymerase picks this. DNA polymerase only assembles new strands on templates that helicase has already exposed.

A student who thinks an enzyme makes the base pairs picks this. Hydrogen bonds between complementary bases form spontaneously; helicase's role is to break them, and without it no strand is even started.
A student who thinks division halves the DNA picks this. Each daughter cell must receive a complete copy of the DNA, so without replication normal division cannot proceed.
questions.explain: Helicase is needed to unwind the helix and break the hydrogen bonds between the strands. Without it the strands stay paired, no template is exposed and DNA polymerase has nothing to copy.

questions.q: A DNA profile was prepared for a mother, her child and a man who may be the father. The fragment lengths (in base pairs) in each profile were: mother 100, 220, 260, 340; child 100, 150, 220, 300; man 150, 180, 300, 330. What can be concluded?
options: The man is excluded as the father, because two of his bands (180 and 330) do not appear in the child's profile.
The man cannot be excluded as the father: the child's two bands not from the mother (150 and 300) are both in his profile.
The man is excluded as the father, because the child's profile does not match his profile completely.
The man is proved to be the father, because DNA profiles are unique and two of his bands match the child's.
optionWhy: A student who expects the child to carry all of the father's bands picks this. A child inherits only half of each parent's DNA, so bands in the father that the child did not inherit are expected.

The child's bands 100 and 220 came from the mother. The remaining bands, 150 and 300, must come from the biological father, and both appear in the man's profile, so he cannot be excluded. Further markers would be used to make the conclusion more reliable.
A student who applies forensic-style complete matching to paternity picks this. Only the child's bands that are not explained by the mother need to be present in the father.
A student who treats any match as proof picks this. Sharing bands at a few markers is consistent with paternity but does not prove it; other men could share the same fragment lengths by chance.
questions.explain: The child's bands 100 and 220 came from the mother. The remaining bands, 150 and 300, must come from the biological father, and both appear in the man's profile, so he cannot be excluded. Further markers would be used to make the conclusion more reliable.

questions.q: On the lagging strand, DNA polymerase III has extended an Okazaki fragment until it reaches the RNA primer of the previous fragment. Which sequence of events completes this section of the strand?
options: DNA ligase joins the new fragment to the RNA primer, and then DNA polymerase I replaces the primer with DNA nucleotides.
DNA polymerase III removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments.
DNA primase replaces its RNA primer with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments together.
DNA polymerase I replaces the RNA primer with DNA nucleotides, and then DNA ligase joins the two fragments together.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the fragments must be joined as soon as they meet picks this. DNA ligase acts last: it seals the nick only after the primer has been replaced with DNA.
A student who credits DNA polymerase III with every polymerase task picks this. Removing and replacing primers is the function of DNA polymerase I, not of DNA polymerase III.
A student who takes DNA primase to be a DNA-making enzyme picks this. Primase makes RNA primers only; it is DNA polymerase I that removes them and replaces them with DNA.

DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA, leaving a nick in the backbone between the last nucleotide it added and the next fragment. DNA ligase then forms the covalent bond that seals the nick.
questions.explain: DNA polymerase I removes the RNA primer and replaces it with DNA, leaving a nick in the backbone between the last nucleotide it added and the next fragment. DNA ligase then forms the covalent bond that seals the nick.

questions.q: Which statement describes the roles of RNA polymerase in transcription?
options: It separates the DNA strands and links RNA nucleotides, positioned by pairing with the template strand, into one RNA strand.
It links RNA nucleotides into a strand once helicase has opened the DNA and a primer has been laid down.
It copies both DNA strands of the gene at the same time, producing a double-stranded RNA molecule from the gene.
It joins amino acids together, one after another, in the order specified by the base sequence of the gene.
optionWhy: RNA polymerase binds to the gene, separates the DNA strands, positions free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing with the template strand and forms the covalent bonds that join them into a single RNA strand.

A student who transfers the replication machinery to transcription picks this. RNA polymerase separates the DNA strands itself and needs no primer; helicase and primase are not involved in transcription.
A student who models transcription on replication picks this. Only one strand, the template strand, is transcribed, and the product is a single strand of RNA.
A student who has swapped transcription and translation picks this. Amino acids are joined during translation on a ribosome; RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides, not amino acids.
questions.explain: RNA polymerase binds to the gene, separates the DNA strands, positions free RNA nucleotides by complementary base pairing with the template strand and forms the covalent bonds that join them into a single RNA strand.

questions.q: A section of the DNA template strand of a gene has the base sequence TACGCAT. What is the base sequence of the RNA transcribed from this section?
options: UACGCAU
AUGCGUA
UAGCGAU
ATGCGTA
optionWhy: A student who copies the template like-for-like, only swapping T for U, picks this. The RNA is complementary to the template strand, not identical to it.
Each RNA base is complementary to the template base opposite it: T pairs with A, A on the template pairs with U, C with G and G with C, giving AUGCGUA.
A student who places uracil opposite thymine, and adenine opposite adenine, picks this. Uracil pairs with adenine on the template; thymine on the template pairs with adenine on the RNA.
A student who applies the DNA pairing rules and writes T opposite A picks this. RNA contains uracil, not thymine, so adenine on the template strand pairs with uracil on the RNA.
questions.explain: Each RNA base is complementary to the template base opposite it: T pairs with A, A on the template pairs with U, C with G and G with C, giving AUGCGUA.

questions.q: Developing red blood cells produce large amounts of the beta chain of haemoglobin, but liver cells produce none, although both cell types contain the gene. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The gene is transcribed in developing red blood cells but not in liver cells, so liver cells make no mRNA for the protein.
Liver cells lost the gene when they differentiated, so they no longer contain the DNA sequence for the beta chain.
Both cell types transcribe the gene, but only red blood cells translate the mRNA into the beta chain polypeptide.
Both cell types make the beta chain, but liver cells break the protein down as soon as it has been produced.
optionWhy: Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression, so a gene that is not transcribed in a cell type gives no mRNA and no polypeptide there.
A student who thinks differentiated cells discard genes picks this. The stem states that both cell types contain the gene; the difference is in whether the gene is transcribed.

A student who locates all control at translation picks this. Transcription is the key stage at which a gene is switched on or off; in liver cells the gene is not transcribed, so there is no mRNA to translate.
A student who believes every gene is expressed in every cell picks this. A liver cell does not make the beta chain at all, because the gene is not transcribed in liver cells.
questions.explain: Not all genes in a cell are expressed at any given time. Transcription is the first stage of gene expression, so a gene that is not transcribed in a cell type gives no mRNA and no polypeptide there.

questions.q: A cell contains many different kinds of tRNA molecule. What is the role of a tRNA during translation?
options: It brings a specific amino acid to the ribosome and pairs its anticodon with the matching codon on the mRNA.
It binds to a codon first and then collects from the cytoplasm whichever amino acid that codon specifies.
It delivers an amino acid and remains bonded to it, becoming part of the finished polypeptide chain.
It carries the mRNA bases that the ribosome converts into the amino acids of the polypeptide.
optionWhy: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so complementary base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.
A student who thinks the codon tells the tRNA what to fetch picks this. The amino acid is attached to the tRNA before it reaches the ribosome; the codon selects which loaded tRNA binds.
A student who thinks tRNAs stay in the chain picks this. Once its amino acid has been joined to the polypeptide by a peptide bond, the tRNA leaves the ribosome and is reused.
A student who thinks amino acids are made from bases picks this. tRNA carries an amino acid, not bases to be converted; the mRNA bases only specify which amino acid is added.
questions.explain: Each tRNA carries a specific amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to the codons for that amino acid, so complementary base pairing at the ribosome delivers the amino acid the codon specifies.

questions.q: An mRNA molecule has the base sequence AUGUUUGCUUAAGGC, read from the first base. The genetic code table gives: AUG methionine (start), UUU phenylalanine, GCU alanine, UAA stop, GGC glycine. How many amino acids are in the polypeptide translated from it?
options: two amino acids
four amino acids
three amino acids
fifteen amino acids
optionWhy: A student who does not count the start codon picks this. AUG codes for methionine as well as marking the start, so methionine, phenylalanine and alanine make three.
A student who reads past the stop codon to include GGC picks this. UAA ends translation, so the glycine codon after it is not translated.

The codons are AUG UUU GCU UAA GGC. AUG gives methionine, UUU phenylalanine and GCU alanine; UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends there and GGC is never translated. The polypeptide has three amino acids.
A student who thinks each base codes for one amino acid picks this. The code is a triplet code, so 15 bases form 5 codons, of which one is a stop codon and only three are translated.
questions.explain: The codons are AUG UUU GCU UAA GGC. AUG gives methionine, UUU phenylalanine and GCU alanine; UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends there and GGC is never translated. The polypeptide has three amino acids.

questions.q: An antibiotic stops the ribosome from moving along the mRNA but does not affect the binding of tRNAs or the formation of peptide bonds. What effect will this have on translation of an mRNA?
options: Only the first peptide bond forms, since the next codon cannot be moved into place for a tRNA to bind.
Translation is unaffected, because all the tRNAs bind along the mRNA before any peptide bonds are formed.
Translation is unaffected, because each tRNA leaves the ribosome before the next one binds to the mRNA.
The chain still grows, because each tRNA stays attached to its amino acid and the next tRNA simply joins onto it.
optionWhy: Two tRNAs can bind and a peptide bond can form between their amino acids, but the chain then grows only if the ribosome moves one codon along so that the used tRNA leaves and the next codon is exposed. Without movement, elongation stops.
A student who pictures all the tRNAs lining up at once picks this. Only two tRNAs are bound at a time, so each further codon has to be brought into the ribosome by stepwise movement.
A student who thinks one tRNA is bound at a time picks this. Even so, the next codon must be moved into the ribosome for the next tRNA to pair with it, and the ribosome cannot move.
A student who thinks tRNAs chain together picks this. tRNAs leave after giving up their amino acid, and new tRNAs bind to codons in the ribosome, which the ribosome must move along the mRNA to reach.
questions.explain: Two tRNAs can bind and a peptide bond can form between their amino acids, but the chain then grows only if the ribosome moves one codon along so that the used tRNA leaves and the next codon is exposed. Without movement, elongation stops.

questions.q: During transcription, RNA polymerase adds each new nucleotide to the free 3' end of the growing RNA strand. What does this mean for the direction of transcription?
options: The RNA is synthesized 5' to 3' while the template strand is read 3' to 5'.
The RNA is synthesized 5' to 3' and the template strand is read in the same 5' to 3' direction.
The RNA is synthesized 3' to 5', because the 3' end is where the chain is being extended.
The RNA can be synthesized in either direction, since nucleotides can be joined at either end.
optionWhy: Adding nucleotides to the 3' end means the RNA grows from its 5' end towards its 3' end, which is what 5' to 3' transcription means. The strands are antiparallel, so the template is read from its 3' end towards its 5' end.
A student who forgets that the strands are antiparallel picks this. The RNA runs opposite to the template it pairs with, so the template is read 3' to 5'.
A student who names the direction by the end being extended picks this. Direction of synthesis is from the first nucleotide (5' end) to the last, so extending the 3' end is 5' to 3' synthesis.
A student who gives strands no direction picks this. RNA polymerase can add only to the 3' hydroxyl, so synthesis is always 5' to 3'.
questions.explain: Adding nucleotides to the 3' end means the RNA grows from its 5' end towards its 3' end, which is what 5' to 3' transcription means. The strands are antiparallel, so the template is read from its 3' end towards its 5' end.

questions.q: Which statement about non-coding sequences in eukaryotic DNA is correct?
options: Non-coding sequences such as introns and telomeres have no function at all and so are never transcribed into RNA.
Every gene codes for a polypeptide, so tRNA and rRNA are both produced by translation of their own mRNA molecules.
The promoter of a gene is transcribed and forms the first codons of the mRNA for that gene.
The genes for tRNA and rRNA are transcribed, but their RNA products are never translated into polypeptides.
optionWhy: A student who equates non-coding with junk picks this. Telomeres protect chromosome ends, promoters regulate expression, and introns are transcribed before being spliced out.
A student who defines a gene by its protein product picks this. tRNA and rRNA are made directly by transcription of their genes and are never translated.
A student who confuses the promoter with the start of the mRNA picks this. The promoter is where RNA polymerase binds; it is a regulator of expression, not part of the coding sequence.

Genes for tRNAs and rRNAs are non-coding in the sense that their products are functional RNA molecules, not polypeptides: they are transcribed but never translated. Introns are also transcribed but are removed before translation, while promoters and telomeres are neither translated nor part of any mRNA.
questions.explain: Genes for tRNAs and rRNAs are non-coding in the sense that their products are functional RNA molecules, not polypeptides: they are transcribed but never translated. Introns are also transcribed but are removed before translation, while promoters and telomeres are neither translated nor part of any mRNA.

questions.q: A eukaryotic gene contains three exons separated by two introns. Which statement describes the mature mRNA produced from this gene?
options: It contains the three exons joined together, with a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail added on.
It contains the three exons only, because the introns were cut out of the DNA before the gene was transcribed.
It contains the two introns joined together, because the exons were the sections removed by splicing.
It contains all five sections, with the cap and tail translated as extra amino acids at each end.
optionWhy: Post-transcriptional modification removes the introns from the pre-mRNA and splices the exons together, and adds a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail that stabilize the transcript. The result is the mature mRNA.
A student who removes introns from the gene picks this. The whole gene, introns included, is transcribed into pre-mRNA; the introns are removed from the RNA, and the DNA is unchanged.
A student who has the names the wrong way round picks this. Exons are expressed and retained; introns are the intervening sequences that are removed.
A student who treats everything on the mRNA as code picks this. The introns are removed, and the cap and tail are not translated; they stabilize the mRNA.
questions.explain: Post-transcriptional modification removes the introns from the pre-mRNA and splices the exons together, and adds a 5' cap and a 3' poly-A tail that stabilize the transcript. The result is the mature mRNA.

questions.q: During elongation, what are the roles of the A, P and E sites of the ribosome?
options: A tRNA carrying the next amino acid enters the A site, the tRNA holding the growing polypeptide is in the P site, and a used tRNA leaves from the E site.
A tRNA enters the ribosome at the E site, moves to the P site where its amino acid is added to the growing chain, and finally leaves the ribosome from the A site.
Only one site is occupied at any one time: a tRNA enters the A site, passes through the P site and then the E site, and leaves before the next tRNA enters.
The tRNAs in all three sites remain attached to their amino acids, so the polypeptide is held to the ribosome by three tRNAs at once.
optionWhy: The A site accepts the incoming tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the codon, the P site holds the tRNA attached to the polypeptide, and after the ribosome moves one codon the tRNA that has given up the chain sits in the E site and exits.
A student who reads E as 'entry' picks this. Entry is at the A site, and the E (exit) site is where a tRNA that has given up its amino acid sits before leaving.
A student who thinks one tRNA is bound at a time picks this. Two tRNAs are bound during peptide bond formation, one in the A site and one in the P site.

A student who thinks tRNAs stay bonded to their amino acids picks this. Only the tRNA in the P site (or, just after a peptide bond forms, the A site) holds the polypeptide; the E-site tRNA has no amino acid.
questions.explain: The A site accepts the incoming tRNA whose anticodon pairs with the codon, the P site holds the tRNA attached to the polypeptide, and after the ribosome moves one codon the tRNA that has given up the chain sits in the E site and exits.

questions.q: Two copies of a gene are mutated at the same point in the coding sequence. In copy X three consecutive bases are inserted; in copy Y one base is inserted. Which comparison is correct?
options: X keeps the reading frame so the codons after it are unchanged, but Y shifts the frame for every later codon
Both X and Y shift the reading frame, so both of the polypeptides are likely to cease to function
Both X and Y alter just one amino acid at the insertion point, leaving the rest unchanged
Y changes every amino acid, including those before the insertion, whereas X adds just one amino acid
optionWhy: Three bases is a whole codon, so in X the codons after the insertion are grouped exactly as before: the polypeptide gains one amino acid (possibly with one adjacent amino acid altered) and the rest is unchanged. One extra base in Y is not a multiple of three, so every later codon is regrouped: a frameshift that is likely to abolish function.

A student who thinks every insertion causes a frameshift picks this. The frame shifts only when the number of bases inserted is not a multiple of three, so X, with three bases inserted, keeps the frame.

A student who assumes one base change means one amino acid change picks this. It is roughly true for X, but the single extra base in Y regroups every codon after it, changing the whole of the rest of the polypeptide.

A student who thinks a frameshift alters the amino acids before the mutation as well picks this. The X clause is correct, but in Y the ribosome reads the codons before the insertion exactly as before; only the codons after it are regrouped.
questions.explain: Three bases is a whole codon, so in X the codons after the insertion are grouped exactly as before: the polypeptide gains one amino acid (possibly with one adjacent amino acid altered) and the rest is unchanged. One extra base in Y is not a multiple of three, so every later codon is regrouped: a frameshift that is likely to abolish function.

questions.q: Cultures of cells were exposed separately to (i) ultraviolet light, (ii) visible light and (iii) nitrous acid, a chemical that alters bases in DNA. Which treatments are expected to raise the mutation rate above the background rate?
options: (i), (ii) and (iii), because light and chemicals both damage DNA
(iii) only, because radiation from non-radioactive sources is harmless
None of them, because DNA repair enzymes correct all of the damage
(i) and (iii), because both chemically alter the bases in DNA
optionWhy: A student who assumes all radiation is mutagenic includes visible light. Visible light does not carry enough energy to alter DNA chemically, so it is not a mutagen; only the ultraviolet light and the chemical raise the mutation rate.

A student who thinks only nuclear radiation is mutagenic picks this. Ultraviolet light is a mutagenic form of radiation whatever its source; sunlight is the main cause of the mutations that lead to skin cancer.
A student who believes repair is perfect picks this. Repair enzymes correct most damage, but mutagens increase the damage so much that more errors escape, and the mutation rate rises measurably.

Ultraviolet light is a mutagenic form of radiation (it causes adjacent thymine bases to bond together) and nitrous acid is a chemical mutagen that alters bases so that they mispair. Visible light does not have enough energy to change DNA.
questions.explain: Ultraviolet light is a mutagenic form of radiation (it causes adjacent thymine bases to bond together) and nitrous acid is a chemical mutagen that alters bases so that they mispair. Visible light does not have enough energy to change DNA.

questions.q: A mutation occurs in a gene that controls the cell cycle in one cell lining a man's colon. Which statement about the consequences is correct?
options: The mutation will be passed on to all of the man's children
The mutation will spread to every cell in the man's body
The cell has become cancerous, as does every mutated somatic cell
The cell may divide uncontrollably and form a tumour
optionWhy: A student who thinks any mutation is heritable picks this. A colon cell is a somatic cell, so its mutation cannot enter a sperm cell and is not inherited.
A student who expects a mutation to spread through the body picks this. The mutation is copied only into the descendants of the one mutated cell when it divides.
A student who equates somatic mutation with cancer picks this. Most somatic mutations do not cause cancer, and even a mutation in a cell-cycle gene raises the risk rather than guaranteeing a tumour.

Genes controlling the cell cycle keep cell division under control. A mutation in such a gene in a somatic cell can allow the cell and its descendants to divide without restraint, which is how cancer begins; several such mutations are usually needed before a tumour forms.
questions.explain: Genes controlling the cell cycle keep cell division under control. A mutation in such a gene in a somatic cell can allow the cell and its descendants to divide without restraint, which is how cancer begins; several such mutations are usually needed before a tumour forms.

questions.q: A direct-to-consumer genetic test reports that a healthy woman carries an SNP associated with a risk of type 2 diabetes 1.5 times higher than that of people without it. Which interpretation is correct?
options: She will certainly develop type 2 diabetes in later life, because she carries the genetic variant that causes the disease
She is more likely than non-carriers to develop the disease, but may never do so; expert interpretation is needed
The test has diagnosed type 2 diabetes in her, so she should begin treatment for the disease immediately
The SNP is a rare disease-causing error in her DNA, so she has inherited a genetic disease from one parent
optionWhy: A student who reads a risk as a prediction picks this. A 1.5-fold risk means the disease is somewhat more likely, not certain, and many carriers never develop it.

The result describes an altered probability, not an outcome. Whether she develops type 2 diabetes also depends on other genes, diet, activity and chance. This is the NOS point: without expert interpretation, information from commercial genetic tests can be problematic.
A student who treats a genetic test like a blood test picks this. The test read her DNA variants; it did not measure her blood glucose or detect any present disease, and she is healthy.
A student who equates SNP with a defective gene picks this. SNPs are common variants; this one shifts the probability of a complex disease and is not a disease-causing mutation.
questions.explain: The result describes an altered probability, not an outcome. Whether she develops type 2 diabetes also depends on other genes, diet, activity and chance. This is the NOS point: without expert interpretation, information from commercial genetic tests can be problematic.

questions.q: Mice in which gene P has been knocked out show no detectable difference from normal mice under standard laboratory conditions. What is the best conclusion?
options: P has no function, because removing its product produced no change in the mice's phenotype
The knockout did not work, because the sequence of P is still present in the genome
The protein made by P is still active because only the gene, not the protein, was altered
P may have a function masked by another gene or shown only in untested conditions
optionWhy: A student who takes a null result as proof picks this. The knockout can only reveal functions that produce a difference under the conditions examined; redundancy and untested conditions can hide a real function.
A student who thinks a knocked-out gene must be absent from the DNA picks this. A gene is knocked out when it is made inoperative; its sequence can remain in the chromosome.
A student who thinks knockout acts on the protein picks this. Making the gene inoperative means no functional protein is produced, so there is no active protein from P in the knockout mice.

Absence of a visible change does not show absence of function. Another gene with a similar product may compensate for the loss, the function may matter only under stress, infection or at other life stages, or the effect may be too subtle for the tests used.
questions.explain: Absence of a visible change does not show absence of function. Another gene with a similar product may compensate for the loss, the function may matter only under stress, infection or at other life stages, or the effect may be too subtle for the tests used.

questions.q: In 2018 a scientist announced the birth of babies whose genomes had been edited with CRISPR–Cas9 at the embryo stage. The work was condemned by scientists worldwide and the scientist was later imprisoned under his own country's laws. Why is there an international effort to harmonize the regulation of genome editing?
options: A single worldwide law on genome editing exists and only needs to be enforced
Once embryo editing is shown to be safe there will be no ethical issue left to regulate
Regulation is national, so a use banned in one country may be legal in another
Editing an embryo is the same as editing adult somatic cells, so no new rules are needed
optionWhy: A student who assumes a global authority already governs this picks this. No such law exists; the scientist was punished under national law, and it is precisely because rules differ between countries that harmonization is being sought.

A student who equates ethical with safe picks this. Consent of future generations, fairness of access and the acceptability of altering human embryos are ethical issues that remain even if the procedure is safe.

Regulation is national, so what is prohibited in one country may be legal or unregulated in another and research could move to the least restrictive jurisdiction. Harmonizing regulation aims to ensure that the ethical issues raised by uses such as heritable embryo editing are addressed before implementation anywhere.

A student who thinks somatic edits are inherited sees no difference between the two. Edits to an embryo enter every cell including the germ line and are passed to descendants; edits to an adult's somatic cells are not, which is why embryo editing raises distinct ethical issues.
questions.explain: Regulation is national, so what is prohibited in one country may be legal or unregulated in another and research could move to the least restrictive jurisdiction. Harmonizing regulation aims to ensure that the ethical issues raised by uses such as heritable embryo editing are addressed before implementation anywhere.
